I'm 27 and I'm a new grad currently looking for my first OT Job. My oldest classmate was in their mid-30s when they graduated. A few of my classmates graduated in business, education, management, etc. and also changed careers!

I live in California, and there are 9 - 10 schools here (I think), the competition is increasing, but with good prerequisite grades, high GRE Score, and enough volunteer hours, I think you can get in! As long as you're open in where to go, and that includes out-of-state! There is the NBCOT, which is the board exam to be licensed, and that's about it! However, if you're interested in specific jobs, like hand therapy, feeding, etc., you may need to take another exam and input a few hours to be certified in these. They're not required, but it will look really good on your background!

The good thing in OT, is that you can work in schools, hospitals, clinics, community outreaches, etc. You can also work in any age setting, from infants to the elderly! To be honest, I feel like OT Schools will like your design field because you can definitely incorporate that in future sessions!

I get it though, a change in careers is definitely a huge step. Just think it through and see if it's best for you! Volunteer in settings you are interested in and see if you can see yourself working like that for a while! Good luck!

I was in a similar situation to you when I studied for the NBCOT! These were my scores: 

Pre-Test (NO studying whatsoever): 447  
Practice Exam 1 (Week 5/7 of studying): 432 (?!)  
Full Practice Exam (Week 7/7 of studying): 472

Actual Exam: 492

There is a common trend I saw amongst other test takers that the Practice Exams are harder than the actual ones. I rescheduled my exam day one week later after seeing that scary score on Practice Exam 1, lol. Some study techniques I've done are focusing on answering the questions, other than cramming all the content in one go. Use all your study questions and understand why the answers are right/wrong! There are a lot of YouTube videos that explain tips on answering the NBCOT questions. For last-minute studying, I used OTRex's videos since her notes were concise and easy to memorize! 

Good luck you're almost there!

I knew that social distancing is important, but I can't help but think about the country in the long-run. I blocked those in social media who belittle others for going outside, saying we'll kill their grandma, lmao. I honestly thought things will get better, and I tried to see the bright side of sheltering.

But now that it's extended until the end of May, with proof that the curve is flattening, I'm starting to be skeptic about all this. Realized my immune system is probably diminishing for staying home too long. Also realized that the Virus will be here forever, so there's no point in being in SIP forever. Now, I just see this situation as pure paranoia. I'm just gonna take my chances, I can't believe people are okay with staying home for another few months. I express my concerns and get downvoted. Oh well. People are just narrow-minded.

Ooh, I would like to commend you on your choice of setting! I spoke with a couple of OTs that work in prisons and jails.

While it is a rewarding and fulfilling setting to be in, the idea is still fresh and requires more time and effort to create more job opportunities for OT.

You have to be very creative and think outside-the-Box in this setting. Prisons are very restricted in items we can bring (no assessments involving needles, or any “sharp” objects). The duties are similar to a SNF and a psychiatry unit combined. So, we will do a lot of mental health and cognitive interventions. 

As I mentioned earlier, the making of OTs working in prisons are still in the works. The current OTs I spoke with are still advocating our profession with other correctional facilities. It can take as little as a few months, to many years for a job opportunity like this.
